Wait, what? The Judge said no such thing. Did you even read the opinion?

http://www.bailii.org/ew/cases/EWHC/Admin/2015/1723.html

The flaw is actually in the government's argument and reasoning behind the law ("regulatory decision" in American-legal speak). I think they should have argued that this was a fair-use right already present in common and that they were just codifying it. Instead, the argument the claimants (evil RIAA and MPAA peoples) are making is that this is creating a "harm" by affecting the copyright. In that case, there is a burden (under law) for the government to assess such "harm". They attempted to assess the potential harm, but the Judge found that the assessment fell short of their burden by being "inconclusive", and the government has the responsibility to overcome the default standing of the assumed "harm". His judgement doesn't nullify the law change. It just gives the government the choice to either change the rule, or perform further assessment to reach a conclusion.

This is actually a loss for the claimants, as all but one of their arguments was denied, and that one is a small burden for the government - they just have to get an independent scientist to be conclusive about "pricing-in".
